arguments.title: Give the rate limiter its own state and break the audit cycle
arguments.spec:
# Refactor: Give the Rate Limiter Its Own State and Break the Audit Cycle

`src/limiter.mjs` is a fixed-window rate limiter whose entire state -- counters, settings, clock -- lives in
module-level `let` bindings, and `src/audit-log.mjs` imports it back to read the configuration in force. Give a
limiter its own state and break the cycle. Change nothing it does. `src/index.mjs` must keep exporting `allow`,
`configure`, `currentConfig`, `setClock`, `reset`, `denials` and `clearDenials` as callable module-level
functions -- callers use them and they are part of the behaviour.

The behaviour, stated precisely (frozen scenarios own these, read them before touching anything):
- `allow(key)` returns `{ allowed, remaining, resetAt }`. A key must be a non-empty string or it throws `TypeError`.
- The window is fixed from the first hit: `resetAt = now + windowMs`. It rolls when `now >= resetAt` -- `resetAt`
  itself already belongs to the new window.
- A denied call does not add a hit, and `remaining` is `0`. Keys are counted independently.
- `configure(next)` merges into the current settings and returns them; it accepts no argument and `undefined`.
  `currentConfig()` returns a copy -- mutating it must not change the limiter.
- A changed limit applies to the window in force as well: it is read at decision time, not captured when the
  window opened.
- `reset()` clears the counters and leaves the settings alone.
- `setClock(fn)` installs a clock; `setClock` with anything that is not a function restores real time.
- Each denial is logged with the key, the time, and the max/windowMs in force at that moment. `denials()` returns
  copies; `clearDenials()` empties the log.

`scenarios/`, `test/refactor.test.js` and `scripts/run-tests.mjs` are FROZEN evidence, digest-checked on every
run. Two things are measured every run: BEHAVIOUR (all 9 frozen scenarios B01-B09 must keep passing exactly as
before) and STRUCTURE, graded against exactly four goals in `refactor/manifest.json`'s `refactor/goals.json`:

- G1 `no_module_level_mutable_state` -- verified against the real fixture: the unmodified tree has four
  module-level `let` bindings (`src/limiter.mjs`'s `counters`, `config`, `clock`; `src/audit-log.mjs`'s
  `entries`). A `const` holding an object you mutate is not flagged; a named instance is a legitimate answer.
- G2 `no_import_cycle` -- verified against the real fixture: the unmodified tree has the 2-node cycle
  `src/audit-log.mjs -> src/limiter.mjs -> src/audit-log.mjs` (the limiter records denials through the audit
  log; the audit log reads the limiter's configuration back).
- G3 `max_function_lines` (limit 15) -- verified against the real fixture: the unmodified `allow` is 19
  meaningful lines.
- G4 `max_branches_per_function` (limit 4, counted as if/case/ternary/&&/||/catch) -- verified against the real
  fixture: the unmodified `allow` has 5 branch points.

The deliverable is `refactor/manifest.json`: `addressed` lists the goal ids genuinely met; every goal listed is
checked immediately and strictly. `complete: true` requires every goal listed and met. `npm test` must pass
exactly as-is, offline -- never add a dependency.

One repair, hand-verified against the real fixture in a scratch copy to satisfy all four goals at once while
leaving all 9 frozen behaviour scenarios passing unchanged (14/14 total, including with `complete: true`):
IMPORTANT non-obvious fact about how functions are measured here -- the verifier detects a function span from its
header line and then skips past its entire body, so a plain function containing nested inner functions gets its
ENTIRE body (every nested function's lines and branches) counted as ONE function. A `class`, by contrast, is
invisible to the detector (the `class Name {` line itself matches nothing), so each METHOD inside it is found
and measured independently. That is why the fix is a class, not a closure-based factory: `export class
RateLimiter` in a new `src/rateLimiter.mjs`, holding `this.counters`, `this.config`, `this.clock` as instance
properties set in the constructor (never module-level bindings), with methods `configure(next)`,
`currentConfig()`, `setClock(nextClock)`, `reset()`, a private-in-spirit `windowFor(key, now)` helper, and
`allow(key)` -- each method verified independently under 15 lines and 4 branches (worst case: `allow` at 13
lines / 3 branches). `src/audit-log.mjs`'s `recordDenial` changes signature to `(key, atMs, max, windowMs)` --
taking the values it needs as arguments instead of importing `currentConfig` back from the limiter -- which
removes the only edge going the wrong way and breaks the cycle; `entries` becomes `const entries = []`, mutated
via `.push`/`.length = 0` instead of reassigned. `src/limiter.mjs` shrinks to a single `const limiter = new
RateLimiter();` plus five thin module-level functions (`allow`, `configure`, `currentConfig`, `setClock`,
`reset`) that each delegate to it -- this is what keeps the module-level convenience functions callable exactly
as before while the state itself lives on the instance. `src/index.mjs` needs no change: it already re-exports
these same names from these same two files.
arguments.plan:
Two cards, chained:

1. `give-limiter-its-own-state-and-break-audit-cycle` -- does the actual restructuring: new src/rateLimiter.mjs
   (an exported RateLimiter class whose methods each measure independently), src/limiter.mjs rewritten to a thin
   module-level wrapper around one named instance, src/audit-log.mjs's recordDenial taking its inputs as
   arguments instead of importing the limiter back. Verified empirically against the real fixture: all 9
   behaviour scenarios (B01-B09) still pass, and claiming G1+G2+G3+G4 against the refactored tree is genuinely
   accepted by the real frozen verifier (worst function 13/15 lines, worst branch count 3/4). This card lists
   all four goals in refactor/manifest.json's `addressed` (leaving `complete: false`) once it has verified them
   itself via a real npm test run in-session.
2. `verify-and-complete-rate-limiter-refactor` (depends on 1) -- independently re-verifies (does not trust the
   previous card) that all four goals are genuinely met via a fresh npm test run, then sets `complete: true`.
arguments.summary: src/limiter.mjs keeps its whole state in module-level `let` bindings and src/audit-log.mjs imports it back, forming a 2-node import cycle. Plan: one card gives the limiter a class-based named instance (each method measures independently under the verifier's function-span detector, unlike a closure-based factory whose nested functions would all be counted as one giant function), and changes the audit log to take its inputs as arguments instead of reading the limiter back -- verified empirically against the real fixture to satisfy all four structural goals at once while keeping all 9 frozen behaviour scenarios passing exactly as before (14/14 including complete:true); one card independently re-verifies and marks the manifest complete. No open assumptions.

tasks.prompt:
Give the rate limiter its own state (a named instance, not module-level bindings) and break
the import cycle with the audit log, without changing a single thing `allow`/`configure`/`currentConfig`/
`setClock`/`reset`/`denials`/`clearDenials` do.

Baseline (verified against the real fixture, not assumed): claiming G1+G2+G3+G4 against the UNMODIFIED tree
fails all four -- src/limiter.mjs has three module-level `let` bindings (`counters`, `config`, `clock`) and
src/audit-log.mjs has one (`entries`); there is a 2-node import cycle
`src/audit-log.mjs -> src/limiter.mjs -> src/audit-log.mjs`; and `allow` is 19 meaningful lines with 5 branch
points.

Read the behaviour section of specification.md and scenarios/limiter.scenarios.mjs (B01-B09) before writing
anything -- the window-rolling rule, the decision-time config read, and the denial-record shape are all
observable and must be reproduced exactly.

IMPORTANT and non-obvious: the verifier finds a function span from its header line and then skips past that
span's ENTIRE body when scanning for the next one. A plain function containing nested inner functions therefore
gets its whole body (every nested function's lines and branches, summed) measured as ONE function -- a
closure-based factory (`function createRateLimiter() { let counters ...; function allow() {...}; ...; return
{...}; }`) would NOT give you small independently-measured methods, it would give you one huge one. A `class`
declaration line itself matches nothing in the detector, so it is invisible to it, and each METHOD inside the
class (which looks like `name(args) {`) IS found and measured independently. Use a class for this reason, not
because of any stylistic preference.

Shape (verified empirically against the real fixture: all 9 frozen behaviour scenarios B01-B09 keep passing
exactly as before, and G1+G2+G3+G4 are all genuinely accepted by the real frozen verifier, including with
`complete: true`):

- New `src/rateLimiter.mjs` exporting `class RateLimiter`. `constructor()` sets `this.counters = new Map()`,
  `this.config = { windowMs: 60000, max: 5 }`, `this.clock = () => Date.now()` (instance properties, never
  module-level bindings). Methods, each a direct transcription of the existing logic onto `this`:
  `configure(next)`, `currentConfig()`, `setClock(nextClock)`, `reset()`, a `windowFor(key, now)` helper (rolls
  the window: reuse the existing one if it exists and `now < existing.resetAt`, otherwise start a fresh one
  `{ hits: 0, resetAt: now + this.config.windowMs }`; store it back into `this.counters` either way; return it),
  and `allow(key)` (validate the key, get `now` from `this.clock()`, get the window via `windowFor`, and if
  `window.hits >= this.config.max` call `recordDenial(key, now, this.config.max, this.config.windowMs)` and
  return the denial, otherwise increment `window.hits` and return the allowance). Import `recordDenial` from
  `src/audit-log.mjs` (a plain one-directional import -- audit-log does not import anything back).
- `src/audit-log.mjs`: change `recordDenial`'s signature to `(key, atMs, max, windowMs)` -- it no longer imports
  `currentConfig` from the limiter, it just records the values it is given. Change `let entries = []` to
  `const entries = []`, and `clearDenials` to `entries.length = 0` instead of reassigning. `denials()` is
  unchanged. This is what removes the cycle: nothing in this file imports from `src/limiter.mjs` or
  `src/rateLimiter.mjs` any more.
- `src/limiter.mjs`: shrinks to `import { RateLimiter } from "./rateLimiter.mjs"; const limiter = new
  RateLimiter();` (a single module-level `const`, not flagged) plus five thin exported functions -- `allow`,
  `configure`, `currentConfig`, `setClock`, `reset` -- each just calling the matching method on `limiter` and
  returning its result. This is what keeps the module-level convenience functions callable exactly as before.
- `src/index.mjs`: no change needed -- it already re-exports these same seven names from these same two files.

Do not change any return shape, the window-rolling rule, or which config values are read at decision time versus
window-open time. Never add a dependency (the sandbox is offline).

whole-file rewrites; do not retry an identical rejected edit_file call more than once -- fall back to
write_file). (3) In a further later turn, run npm test and confirm every one of the 9 behaviour scenarios

flip belongs to the card that depends on this one. Re-read to confirm, then run npm test once more (never in the
